claim: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) accounts for 25–30% of all leukemias in the Western countries.
source: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) accounts for 25–30% of all leukemias in the Western countries, with incidence rates ranging from 3.65 to 6.75 cases per 100,000 population per year (Siegel et al., 2019; Sant et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Siegel et al., 2019 and Sant et al., 2010.

claim: CLL has incidence rates ranging from 3.65 to 6.75 cases per 100,000 population per year.
source: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) accounts for 25–30% of all leukemias in the Western countries, with incidence rates ranging from 3.65 to 6.75 cases per 100,000 population per year (Siegel et al., 2019; Sant et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Siegel et al., 2019 and Sant et al., 2010.

claim: CLL is characterized by an outgrowth of malignant CD5 positive B cells.
source: CLL is characterized by an outgrowth of malignant CD5 positive B cells, mainly residing in the peripheral blood (PB), bone marrow, and lymphoid organs, and by a high biological heterogeneity reflected in clinically different outcomes including disease progression, therapy response, and relapse (Kröber et al., 2002; Zenz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kröber et al., 2002 and Zenz et al., 2010.

claim: Malignant CD5 positive B cells in CLL mainly reside in the peripheral blood (PB), bone marrow, and lymphoid organs.
source: CLL is characterized by an outgrowth of malignant CD5 positive B cells, mainly residing in the peripheral blood (PB), bone marrow, and lymphoid organs, and by a high biological heterogeneity reflected in clinically different outcomes including disease progression, therapy response, and relapse (Kröber et al., 2002; Zenz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kröber et al., 2002 and Zenz et al., 2010.

claim: CLL exhibits high biological heterogeneity reflected in clinically different outcomes including disease progression, therapy response, and relapse.
source: CLL is characterized by an outgrowth of malignant CD5 positive B cells, mainly residing in the peripheral blood (PB), bone marrow, and lymphoid organs, and by a high biological heterogeneity reflected in clinically different outcomes including disease progression, therapy response, and relapse (Kröber et al., 2002; Zenz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kröber et al., 2002 and Zenz et al., 2010.

claim: The hallmark of CLL disease is mainly decreased apoptosis resulting from overexpression of anti-apoptotic proteins and resistance to apoptosis in vivo.
source: The hallmark of the CLL disease is mainly decreased apoptosis resulting from overexpression of anti-apoptotic proteins and resistance to apoptosis in vivo.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about CLL.

claim: The Tcl1 oncogene is highly expressed in CLL cells.
source: The Tcl1 oncogene is highly expressed in CLL cells, and its expression level correlates with the CLL aggressiveness (Herling et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herling et al., 2006.

claim: Tcl1 expression level correlates with CLL aggressiveness.
source: The Tcl1 oncogene is highly expressed in CLL cells, and its expression level correlates with the CLL aggressiveness (Herling et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herling et al., 2006.

claim: Tcl1 was initially discovered as a gene involved in the rearrangement of the T-cell leukemia/lymphoma 1 locus at 14q32.1.
source: Tcl1 was initially discovered as a gene involved in the rearrangement of the T-cell leukemia/lymphoma 1 locus at 14q32.1, the most common chromosomal aberrations detected in mature T-cell leukemias (Virgilio et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Virgilio et al., 1994.

claim: The rearrangement at 14q32.1 is the most common chromosomal aberration detected in mature T-cell leukemias.
source: Tcl1 was initially discovered as a gene involved in the rearrangement of the T-cell leukemia/lymphoma 1 locus at 14q32.1, the most common chromosomal aberrations detected in mature T-cell leukemias (Virgilio et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Virgilio et al., 1994.

claim: The central role of TCL1 in CLL was demonstrated in transgenic mice overexpressing the human Tcl1 gene under the control of the immunoglobulin promoter and enhancer (Eµ-Tcl1).
source: The central role of TCL1 in CLL was demonstrated in transgenic mice overexpressing the human Tcl1 gene under the control of the immunoglobulin promoter and enhancer (Eµ-Tcl1) (Bichi et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bichi et al., 2002.

claim: Eµ-Tcl1 mice develop normally into adulthood but develop CLL that is highly similar to the human disease.
source: These mice develop normally into adulthood but develop CLL that is highly similar to the human disease and is characterized by CD5+ cells, which accumulate in the spleens, livers, and lymph nodes.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from the Eµ-Tcl1 mouse model.

claim: CLL in Eµ-Tcl1 mice is characterized by CD5+ cells, which accumulate in the spleens, livers, and lymph nodes.
source: These mice develop normally into adulthood but develop CLL that is highly similar to the human disease and is characterized by CD5+ cells, which accumulate in the spleens, livers, and lymph nodes.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from the Eµ-Tcl1 mouse model.

claim: High TCL1 expression is associated with malignant transformation through enhancement of AKT activity.
source: The association of high TCL1 expression and malignant transformation is linked to its involvement in several major oncogenic pathways, including the enhancement of AKT activity (Herling et al., 2008; Noh et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2020; Pekarsky et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Herling et al., 2008; Noh et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2020; Pekarsky et al., 2010.

claim: TCL1 interacts with the DNA repair ataxia–telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) factor.
source: The association of high TCL1 expression and malignant transformation is linked to its involvement in several major oncogenic pathways, including the enhancement of AKT activity (Herling et al., 2008; Noh et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2020; Pekarsky et al., 2010); interaction with the DNA repair ataxia–telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) factor (Gaudio et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gaudio et al., 2012.

claim: TCL1 interacts with the transcription factor CREB.
source: The association of high TCL1 expression and malignant transformation is linked to its involvement in several major oncogenic pathways, including the enhancement of AKT activity (Herling et al., 2008; Noh et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2020; Pekarsky et al., 2010); interaction with the DNA repair ataxia–telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) factor (Gaudio et al., 2012), and the transcription factor CREB (Pekarsky et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pekarsky et al., 2008.

claim: TCL1 contributes to accelerated tumorigenic and the prosurvival NF-κB signaling.
source: The association of high TCL1 expression and malignant transformation is linked to its involvement in several major oncogenic pathways, including the enhancement of AKT activity (Herling et al., 2008; Noh et al., 2012; Patil et al., 2020; Pekarsky et al., 2010); interaction with the DNA repair ataxia–telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) factor (Gaudio et al., 2012), and the transcription factor CREB (Pekarsky et al., 2008) as well as in contributing to accelerated tumorigenic and the prosurvival NF-κB signaling (Gaudio et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gaudio et al., 2012.

claim: TCL1 inhibits activator protein 1 (AP-1) transcriptional activity via interaction with the AP-1 complex.
source: Inhibition of activator protein 1 (AP-1) transcriptional activity via interaction of TCL1 with the AP-1 complex represents another mechanism to antagonize the expression of pro-apoptotic factors (Gaudio et al., 2012; Motiwala et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gaudio et al., 2012 and Motiwala et al., 2011.

claim: TCL1 contributes to epigenetic reprogramming via interacting with the de novo DNA methyltransferase 3A (DNMT3A) and reducing its enzymatic activity.
source: TCL1 was also shown to contribute to epigenetic reprogramming via interacting with the de novo DNA methyltransferase 3A (DNMT3A) and reducing its enzymatic activity (Palamarchuk et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Palamarchuk et al., 2012.

claim: Alterations in transcription start site (TSS) selection and alternative promoter (AP) usage increase transcriptome diversity and regulation.
source: Alterations in transcription start site (TSS) selection and alternative promoter (AP) usage increase transcriptome diversity and regulation.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about TSS and AP usage.

claim: mRNA isoforms with different 5′ leaders can vary in their translation efficiency (TE) or half-lives.
source: In addition, mRNA isoforms with different 5′ leaders can vary in their translation efficiency (TE) or half-lives.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about mRNA isoforms.

claim: AP usage can lead to the generation of protein isoforms that differ in their N termini and can have different or even opposite biological functions.
source: Likewise, AP usage can lead to the generation of protein isoforms that differ in their N termini and as a result can have different or even opposite biological functions.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about AP usage.

claim: Recent large-scale promoter analysis in hundreds of human and mouse primary cell types shed light on the prevalence of AP usage in mammals.
source: Recent large-scale promoter analysis in hundreds of human and mouse primary cell types shed light on the prevalence of AP usage in mammals (Forrest et al., 2014) as well as in multiple cancer types (Demircioğlu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Forrest et al., 2014 and Demircioğlu et al., 2019.

claim: Transient cellular stress is associated with dramatic changes in the landscape of TSSs and AP usage that are coordinated with translation.
source: Considering that even transient cellular stress is associated with dramatic changes in the landscape of TSSs and AP usage that are coordinated with translation (Tamarkin-Ben-Harush et al., 2017), it is reasonable to assume that such alterations can affect translatability in cells undergoing oncogenic transformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tamarkin-Ben-Harush et al., 2017.

claim: This study examined the changes in TSS selection and AP usage and their impact on the translatome during malignant transformation of B cells by the Tcl1 oncogene.
source: This study examined the changes in TSS selection and AP usage and their impact on the translatome during malignant transformation of B cells by the Tcl1 oncogene.
evidence: The claim describes the objective of the study.

claim: A marked elevation of APs was revealed in malignant CLL B cells from Eµ-Tcl1 transgenic mice.
source: Our findings revealed a marked elevation of APs in malignant CLL B cells with a particularly high prevalence of intra-genic promoters that are predicted to generate N-terminally truncated or N-terminally modified proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: Intra-genic promoters in CLL B cells are particularly enriched and predicted to generate N-terminally truncated or modified proteins.
source: Our findings revealed a marked elevation of APs in malignant CLL B cells with a particularly high prevalence of intra-genic promoters that are predicted to generate N-terminally truncated or N-terminally modified proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: Intra-genic promoter activation is mediated by loss of function of 'closed chromatin' epigenetic regulators due to the generation of inactive N-terminally modified isoforms or reduced expression.
source: Intra-genic promoter activation is mediated by (1) loss of function of 'closed chromatin' epigenetic regulators due to the generation of inactive N-terminally modified isoforms or reduced expression; (2) upregulation of transcription factors, including c-Myc, targeting the intra-genic promoters and their associated enhancers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: Intra-genic promoter activation is mediated by upregulation of transcription factors, including c-Myc, targeting the intra-genic promoters and their associated enhancers.
source: Intra-genic promoter activation is mediated by (1) loss of function of 'closed chromatin' epigenetic regulators due to the generation of inactive N-terminally modified isoforms or reduced expression; (2) upregulation of transcription factors, including c-Myc, targeting the intra-genic promoters and their associated enhancers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: Exogenous expression of Tcl1 in MEFs is sufficient to induce intra-genic promoters of epigenetic regulators and promote c-Myc expression.
source: Exogenous expression of Tcl1 in MEFs is sufficient to induce intra-genic promoters of epigenetic regulators and promote c-Myc expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: A dramatic translation downregulation of transcripts bearing CNY cap-proximal trinucleotides was found, reminiscent of cells undergoing metabolic stress.
source: We further found a dramatic translation downregulation of transcripts bearing CNY cap-proximal trinucleotides, reminiscent of cells undergoing metabolic stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: These findings uncovered the role of Tcl1 oncogenic function in altering promoter usage and mRNA translation in leukemogenesis.
source: These findings uncovered the role of Tcl1 oncogenic function in altering promoter usage and mRNA translation in leukemogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings as stated in the abstract.

claim: An average of 10.625 million CAGE tags per sample was aligned to a total of 2.67 million CAGE-derived TSSs (CTSSs).
source: An average of 10.625 million CAGE tags per sample was aligned to a total of 2.67 million CAGE-derived TSSs (CTSSs) that were mapped and clustered to a consensus set of 28,616 promoters that correspond to a total of 11,515 genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: CTSSs were mapped and clustered to a consensus set of 28,616 promoters that correspond to a total of 11,515 genes.
source: An average of 10.625 million CAGE tags per sample was aligned to a total of 2.67 million CAGE-derived TSSs (CTSSs) that were mapped and clustered to a consensus set of 28,616 promoters that correspond to a total of 11,515 genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: Metagene analysis of both WT and Eµ-Tcl1 CAGE data showed almost perfect alignment to the annotated TSS atlas of the FANTOM5 project.
source: Metagene analysis of both WT and Eµ-Tcl1 CAGE data showed almost perfect alignment to the annotated TSS atlas of the FANTOM5 project (Lizio et al., 2015; Figure 1B), indicating the proper calculation of the TSS positions at a single-base resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1B, with citation to Lizio et al., 2015.

claim: The reproducibility of the CAGE library replicates was found to be high.
source: The CAGE libraries were assessed with coefficient scores calculated using the Pearson pairwise-correlation test and the reproducibility of the replicates were found to be high (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In both WT and Eµ-Tcl1 samples, most of the TSSs with the highest expression level were mapped to the core promoter region.
source: As expected, in both WT and Eµ-Tcl1 samples, most of the TSSs with the highest expression level were mapped to the core promoter region (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1C.

claim: A significant fraction of the TSSs was found within introns and intergenic regions.
source: A significant fraction of the TSSs was found within introns and intergenic regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: Most of the intronic TSSs (85% in Eµ-Tcl1 and 79% in WT) are derived from eRNAs.
source: Based on the criteria of balanced bidirectional read mapping, we calculated the frequencies of eRNAs in introns and intergenic regions and found that most of the intronic TSSs (85% in Eµ-Tcl1 and 79% in WT) and a significant fraction of the intra-genic TSSs (62% in Eµ-Tcl1 and 50% in WT) are indeed derived from eRNAs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1C.

claim: A significant fraction of the intra-genic TSSs (62% in Eµ-Tcl1 and 50% in WT) are derived from eRNAs.
source: Based on the criteria of balanced bidirectional read mapping, we calculated the frequencies of eRNAs in introns and intergenic regions and found that most of the intronic TSSs (85% in Eµ-Tcl1 and 79% in WT) and a significant fraction of the intra-genic TSSs (62% in Eµ-Tcl1 and 50% in WT) are indeed derived from eRNAs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1C.

claim: PCA1 explained 85% of the variance and distinguished between WT and Eµ-Tcl1.
source: PCA1 explained 85% of the variance and distinguished between WT and Eµ-Tcl1, where WT samples are tightly clustered and Eµ-Tcl1 are separated by 13% of the variance, which is explained by PCA2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Out of the 28,616 consensus TSSs, 3337 were upregulated and 1829 were downregulated in Eµ-Tcl1.
source: Out of the 28,616 consensus TSSs, we found in Eµ-Tcl1 3337 upregulated and 1829 downregulated TSSs (Figure 1D), suggesting an overall upregulation of many promoters in CLL.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1D.

claim: There is an overall upregulation of many promoters in CLL.
source: Out of the 28,616 consensus TSSs, we found in Eµ-Tcl1 3337 upregulated and 1829 downregulated TSSs (Figure 1D), suggesting an overall upregulation of many promoters in CLL.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data showing more upregulated than downregulated TSSs.

claim: 255 eRNAs were upregulated in Eµ-Tcl1, of which 106 were positively correlated to 203 upregulated TSSs.
source: We found 255 upregulated eRNAs, of them 106 were positively correlated to the 203 upregulated TSSs, while out of 179 downregulated eRNAs, 86 were positively correlated to the 331 downregulated TSSs (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1D.

claim: Out of 179 downregulated eRNAs, 86 were positively correlated to 331 downregulated TSSs.
source: We found 255 upregulated eRNAs, of them 106 were positively correlated to the 203 upregulated TSSs, while out of 179 downregulated eRNAs, 86 were positively correlated to the 331 downregulated TSSs (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1D.

claim: General TSSs are characterized by YR at the (−1) and (+1) positions.
source: Consistent with known promoter architecture (Carninci et al., 2006; Suzuki et al., 2001), general TSSs are characterized by YR at the (−1) and (+1) positions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, and citations to Carninci et al., 2006 and Suzuki et al., 2001.

claim: Promoters with broad TSS distributions tend to be surrounded by CpG islands.
source: Promoters with broad TSS distributions tend to be surrounded by CpG islands, while promoters with sharp TSSs are defined by the presence of a TATA box around position −30 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Promoters with sharp TSSs are defined by the presence of a TATA box around position −30.
source: Promoters with broad TSS distributions tend to be surrounded by CpG islands, while promoters with sharp TSSs are defined by the presence of a TATA box around position −30 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Upregulated sharp TSSs showed enrichment of poly-pyrimidine sequence at the positions of +2 to +12.
source: Separately plotted LOGOs of differentially expressed TSSs, showed enrichment of poly-pyrimidine sequence in the upregulated sharp TSSs at the positions of +2 to +12 (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1E.

claim: 2530 genes (22%) contain more than one promoter that contributes over 10% of their total gene expression.
source: We analyzed AP usage in our data and found that 2530 genes (22%) contain more than one promoter that contributes over 10% of their total gene expression (Figure 2B), consistent with previous studies (Tamarkin-Ben-Harush et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis, Figure 2B, and citation to Tamarkin-Ben-Harush et al., 2017.

claim: 550 significant DTUs from 489 genes have alternative TSS upregulated in Eµ-Tcl1.
source: To determine differential TSS usage (DTU), we examined the multipromoter subset and found 550 significant DTUs from 489 genes where the alternative TSS is upregulated in Eµ-Tcl1 and 373 DTUs from 328 genes with downregulated alternative TSS.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: 373 DTUs from 328 genes have downregulated alternative TSS in Eµ-Tcl1.
source: To determine differential TSS usage (DTU), we examined the multipromoter subset and found 550 significant DTUs from 489 genes where the alternative TSS is upregulated in Eµ-Tcl1 and 373 DTUs from 328 genes with downregulated alternative TSS.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: DTU during CLL transformation is gaining more new isoforms than losing the canonical ones.
source: The 47% more cases of upregulated alternative TSS indicate that DTU during CLL transformation is gaining more new isoforms than losing the canonical ones (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data showing 47% more upregulated alternative TSSs.

claim: The Eµ-Tcl1 upregulated alternative TSSs were enriched at the core promoter, 5′ UTR, CDS, and intron regions but not at distal regions.
source: The Eµ-Tcl1 upregulated alternative TSSs were enriched at the core promoter, 5′ UTR, CDS, and intron regions but not at distal regions (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 2C.

claim: A clear elevation in eRNA frequencies was found in Eµ-Tcl1 upregulated alternative TSSs.
source: By analyzing the correlation between alternative TSSs and nearby active enhancers, which are marked by eRNAs, a clear elevation in eRNA frequencies was found in Eµ-Tcl1 upregulated alternative TSSs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Active enhancers play a significant role in the activation of DTUs in Eµ-Tcl1.
source: These findings suggest the significant role of active enhancers in the activation of DTUs in Eµ-Tcl1.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the correlation between eRNA frequencies and upregulated alternative TSSs.

claim: Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) has an intra-genic alternative TSS generating a protein isoform lacking the Ig-like extracellular domains, specifically expressed in WT B cells and predicted to be inactive.
source: This gene has an intra-genic alternative TSS generating a protein isoform lacking the Ig-like extracellular domains of PD-L2 (Latchman et al., 2001; Li et al., 2018; Zak et al., 2017), specifically expressed in WT B cells and is predicted to be inactive.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and citations to Latchman et al., 2001; Li et al., 2018; Zak et al., 2017.

claim: The full-length PD-L2 protein is exclusively expressed in the CLL cells via promoter shift and likely contributes to immunosuppression.
source: In contrast, the full-length protein is exclusively expressed in the CLL cells via promoter shift and likely contributes to immunosuppression (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 2D, with speculation about immunosuppression.

claim: Promoter shifting in Chd1 in Eµ-Tcl1 results in truncation of several critical active domains, presumably leading to loss of function.
source: An opposite example is chromodomain 1 (Chd1), in which promoter shifting in Eµ-Tcl1 is within an intra-genic alternative TSS that results in truncation of several critical active domains, presumably leading to loss of function (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 2E, with speculation about loss of function.

claim: Fbxo5 has two promoters located upstream to the main ORF differing only by their 5′ UTR length resulting in 490 nt shorter 5′ UTR in the Eµ-Tcl1-specific transcript isoform.
source: The F-box only protein 5 (Fbxo5) has two promoters located upstream to the main ORF differing only by their 5′ UTR length resulting in 490 nt shorter 5′ UTR in the Eµ-Tcl1-specific transcript isoform (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 2F.

claim: The upregulated alternative TSS isoforms predicted to give rise to proteins with alternative/truncated N termini are dramatically increased in the Eµ-Tcl1 samples compared to WT B cells.
source: Global analysis of the promoter shifts levels and its significance of all DTUs revealed that the upregulated alternative TSS isoforms predicted to give rise to proteins with alternative/truncated N termini are dramatically increased in the Eµ-Tcl1 samples compared to WT B cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 2G.

claim: This finding suggests a previously unappreciated diversity of the CLL proteome.
source: This finding suggests a previously unappreciated diversity of the CLL proteome.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the finding of dramatically increased alternative TSS isoforms.

claim: GO analysis of genes affected by AP usage shows enrichment in critical CLL pathways, for example, NF-κB signaling, MAPK signaling, Toll-like receptor signaling, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signaling, chromatin regulation/acetylation.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of genes affected by AP usage shows enrichment in critical CLL pathways, for example, NF-κB signaling (Pekarsky et al., 2008), MAPK signaling (Shukla et al., 2018), Toll-like receptor signaling (Spaner and Masellis, 2007), phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signaling (Barragán et al., 2002), chromatin regulation/acetylation, and other relevant GOs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the GO analysis and citations to Pekarsky et al., 2008; Shukla et al., 2018; Spaner and Masellis, 2007; Barragán et al., 2002.

claim: 34 chromatin remodelers with ORF-retaining or -truncating alternative TSSs were found in Eµ-Tcl1 data, 28 of them were upregulated.
source: Our Eµ-Tcl1 data found 34 chromatin remodelers with ORF-retaining or -truncating alternative TSSs that could be classified into factors associated with open or close chromatin states, 28 of them were upregulated in Eµ-Tcl1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 3A.

claim: Most of the upregulated alternative TSS within coding regions of chromatin modifiers are predicted to express truncated proteins that cause loss of critical domains due to DTU.
source: Remarkably, most of the upregulated alternative TSS within coding regions of chromatin modifiers, such as the known key epigenetic gatekeepers such as Hdac4, Hdac5, Sirt2, Smyd4, Kdm4a, Dnmt3a, Chd1, and Mgmt, are predicted to express truncated proteins that cause loss of critical domains due to DTU (Figure 3A and 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figures 3A and 5D.

claim: 5′ RACE-qPCR validation showed dramatic upregulation of the isoforms originating by alternative TSS of Dnmt3a, Chd1, Kdm4a, and Sirt2.
source: To validate the CAGE data, we picked four chromatin modifiers and analyzed them by 5′ RACE-qPCR using RNA samples from Eμ-Tcl1 mice CLL B cells. The results of the 5′ RACE show dramatic upregulation of the isoforms originating by alternative TSS of the four selected Dnmt3a, Chd1, Kdm4a, and Sirt2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the 5′ RACE-qPCR validation data and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Numerous other epigenetic regulators of closed chromatin structure are strongly downregulated in Eµ-Tcl1 B cells.
source: In addition to the truncated chromatin modifiers, numerous other epigenetic regulators of closed chromatin structure are strongly downregulated (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: These findings revealed widespread chromatin deregulation in Eµ-Tcl1 B cells that can activate cryptic promoters.
source: These findings revealed widespread chromatin deregulation in Eµ-Tcl1 B cells that can activate cryptic promoters.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the findings of truncated chromatin modifiers and downregulated epigenetic regulators.

claim: Exogenous expression of hTCL1 in MEFs induces a significant elevation of the intra-genic truncating TSS of Hdac5, Dnmt3a, and Kdm4a but not Zswim4.
source: We observed a significant elevation of the intra-genic truncating TSS of Hdac5, Dnmt3a, and Kdm4a but not Zswim4.
evidence: The claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data from MEFs expressing hTCL1.

claim: Tcl1 itself can promote relaxation of the chromatin structure and promoter shifts, at least in some genes.
source: These findings suggest that Tcl1 itself can promote relaxation of the chromatin structure and promoter shifts, at least in some genes.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the MEF experiment showing induction of intra-genic TSSs by hTCL1.

claim: 63 TFBS were enriched in the promoters of the upregulated alternative TSSs compared to the promoters of the canonical upregulated TSS in Eµ-Tcl1.
source: Using Fisher's exact test, we found 63 TFBS enriched in the promoters of the upregulated alternative TSSs compared to the promoters of the canonical upregulated TSS in Eµ-Tcl1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the TFBS enrichment analysis and Figure 4B.

claim: Upregulated levels of the proto-oncogenes Ets2 and c-Myc correspond to the highly enriched Ets-related and bHLH motifs, respectively.
source: When we combine these data with the list of upregulated TFs in Eµ-Tcl1 (Supplementary file 3), we found that upregulated levels of the proto-oncogenes Ets2 and c-Myc correspond to the highly enriched Ets-related and bHLH motifs, respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined analysis of TFBS enrichment and upregulated TFs, with Figure 4B.

claim: c-Myc is among the upregulated TFs in CAGE data of Eµ-Tcl1 CLL.
source: As c-Myc is among the upregulated TFs in our CAGE data of Eµ-Tcl1 CLL and is predicted to regulate intra-genic APs, we asked whether Tcl1 itself can activate c-Myc.
evidence: The claim is supported by the CAGE data analysis.

claim: The levels of c-Myc are dramatically upregulated in all the hTCL1 expressing MEF clones.
source: Using the hTCL1 MEFs clones, we found that the levels c-Myc are dramatically upregulated in all the hTCL1 expressing clones, indicating that its activation in Eµ-Tcl1 B CLL is most likely intrinsic.
evidence: The claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data from MEFs expressing hTCL1.

claim: c-Myc activation in Eµ-Tcl1 B CLL is most likely intrinsic.
source: Using the hTCL1 MEFs clones, we found that the levels c-Myc are dramatically upregulated in all the hTCL1 expressing clones, indicating that its activation in Eµ-Tcl1 B CLL is most likely intrinsic.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the finding that hTCL1 expression in MEFs upregulates c-Myc.

claim: Nine enriched motifs were found in the upregulated enhancers in Eµ-Tcl1.
source: As many of the upregulated alternative TSSs in Eµ-Tcl1 are associated with active enhancers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), we analyzed TFBS enrichment also in the upregulated enhancers and found nine enriched motifs (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the TFBS enrichment analysis and Figure 4D.

claim: The TFs linked to the nine enriched motifs in upregulated enhancers are all upregulated in the Eµ-Tcl1.

claim: The high monosome to polysome ratio is reminiscent of a state of translation initiation halt, suggesting that protein synthesis capacity is limited in Eµ-Tcl1 CLL cells.

claim: The vast majority of the transcriptionally upregulated DTU (60/76) are classified as High-TE.
source: Intriguingly, the vast majority of the transcriptionally upregulated DTU (60/76) are classified as High-TE, and most of the downregulated DTUs are classified as Low-TE (41/66) (Figure 5C), indicating for coordination of TSS selection with mRNA translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 5C.

claim: Most of the downregulated DTUs are classified as Low-TE (41/66).

evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 5C.

claim: There is coordination of TSS selection with mRNA translation.

claim: 73 intra-genic alternative TSS are upregulated in Eµ-Tcl1 and exceed 50% of the canonical TSS in the polysome fraction.

claim: 168 intra-genic alternative TSS have lower translatability and will less likely impact protein functionality.

claim: Eµ-Tcl1-specific cryptic transcription within the fourth intron of Dnmt3a leads to the loss of three exons (211 amino acids) that constitute its DNA-binding domain.
source: For example, Eµ-Tcl1-specific cryptic transcription (2.22 log FC) within the fourth intron of Dnmt3a leads to the loss of three exons (211 amino acids) that constitute its DNA-binding domain (Figure 5F), which is important to the DNA methylation activity (Suetake et al., 2011) and is generally associated with closed chromatin state (Brocks et al., 2017).

claim: The Dnmt3a DNA-binding domain is important to the DNA methylation activity.

claim: A promoter shifting in Sirt2 interrupts the deacetylase domain positioned between residues 65 and 340 that generates a truncated isoform with higher translatability compared to the canonical isoform.
source: A promoter shifting in Sirtuin 2 (Sirt2, 3.32 log FC), a type III histone deacetylase (Hdac), interrupts the deacetylase domain positioned between residues 65 and 340 that generates a truncated isoform with higher translatability compared to the canonical isoform which is enriched in the polysomes fraction (Figure 5F. middle).

claim: Eµ-Tcl1 B cells are characterized by reduced eraser activities of histone acetylation and methylation, to maintain open chromatin state.
source: Thus, with five truncated members of the HDAC and KDM families (Hdac4, Hdac5, Sirt2 and Sirt4, Kdm4a) and dramatic downregulation of Hdac11 and Hdac9 (−13.79 and −4.59 log FC, respectively, Table 1), it appears that Eµ-Tcl1 B cells are characterized by reduced eraser activities of histone acetylation and methylation, to maintain open chromatin state.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the findings of truncated HDACs and KDMs and downregulated Hdac11 and Hdac9.

claim: The frequency of A and G as TSS nucleotides (47% and 36%, respectively) is higher than C and T (9% and 4%, respectively) in Eµ-Tcl1.
source: We first determined the frequencies of TSS nucleotides in our Eµ-Tcl1 data and found that the frequency of A and G (47% and 36%, respectively) is higher than the C and T (9% and 4%, respectively), as expected (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 6A.

claim: In Eµ-Tcl1, purines account for 83%, but in MEFs, only 64%.
source: Yet, the difference between purines to pyrimidines is substantially more significant. For example, in Eµ-Tcl1, purines account for 83%, but in MEFs, only 64% (Tamarkin-Ben-Harush et al., 2017), suggesting an increased preference of purines as start sites in B CLL cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and citation to Tamarkin-Ben-Harush et al., 2017.

claim: Transcripts initiated with a 'C' have a substantially lower TE compared to A, G, and T.
source: We next determined the TE of transcripts with different initiating nucleotides and observed that those initiated with a 'C' have a substantially lower TE compared to the A, G, and T (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 6B.

claim: Almost all C initiating trinucleotides have a relatively lower TE.
source: To examine whether the lower TE associated with the cap-proximal C is linked to the well-known TOP element (CYYYY), we analyzed the TE of the first trinucleotides and found that almost all C initiating trinucleotides have a relatively lower TE, including inhibitory trinucleotides that are part of the TOP element such as CCT and CTT, but also others that deviate from the TOP such as CAC, CAT, and CTG.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis of the first trinucleotides.

claim: Among the C-initiating triplets, those with a pyrimidine (CNY) in the third position are associated with a much lower TE.
source: Interestingly, among the C-initiating triplets, those with a pyrimidine (CNY) in the third position are associated with a much lower TE (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 6C.

claim: The nucleotides that follow the CNY do not seem to contribute to the TE suppression.
source: Importantly, the nucleotides that follow the CNY do not seem to contribute to the TE suppression (Figure 6D), indicating that the CNY context is the predominant feature.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 6D.

source: Importantly, the nucleotides that follow the CNY do not seem to contribute to the TE suppression (Figure 6D), indicating that the CNY context is the predominant feature.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the finding that nucleotides following CNY do not contribute to TE suppression.

claim: In energy-starved MEFs, the CNY is also associated with more significant inhibition of the TE.
source: A previous study that analyzed the relationship between the first nucleotide and the relative TE also reported that 'C' initiating transcripts are associated with lower TE, particularly following energy stress (Tamarkin-Ben-Harush et al., 2017). We reanalyzed these previous data and found that in energy-starved MEFs, the CNY is also associated with more significant inhibition of the TE (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the reanalysis of previous data and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B, with citation to Tamarkin-Ben-Harush et al., 2017.

claim: The higher monosome-to-polysome ratio and the association of 'CNY' with reduced TE are consistent with Eµ-Tcl1 B CLL cells being under metabolic stress.

evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the polysome profiling data and the CNY-TE association.

source: We found that the non-CLL or healthy B cells were inhibited by the HDAC2A and eIF4E inhibitors in a dose-dependent manner, whereas the CLL cells displayed reduced sensitivity (Figure 7).

claim: None of the B-cell types was affected by inhibitors against HDAC3A and KDM4A at the concentrations used.

evidence: The claim is supported by the survival assay data.

evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the finding that CLL cells displayed reduced sensitivity to inhibitors.
